title: Op art
summary: Black and white stripes, checks, and rings so tight that the surface seems to move. The 1960s optical look.
lede: Optical art as a design style: hard-edged geometric patterns in black and white, such as parallel stripes, checkerboards, and concentric rings, set so close and so sharp that the eye sees vibration, swelling, and moiré. The movement peaked in 1964–1966 in painting and passed at once into fashion, textiles, and graphic design. This record covers that black-and-white graphic core. Color op painting (Anuszkiewicz, Riley after 1967) and kinetic art are related branches.

era.note: Wikidata gives 1960 as the start. Time magazine named the style in October 1964, and MoMA’s The Responsive Eye opened in February 1965. The V&A dates the op-art fashion trend to 1965. Vasarely’s Zebras (1938) is an early precursor.

Wikipedia: Op art (term coined by Time, 1964; The Responsive Eye, 1965; Grignani’s graphic design)
V&A: Biba mini-dress, 1965 (O133328), catalogued with the style “Op art” and dated to “the short lived Op Art fashion trend of 1965”

AIGA Eye on Design: “The Hypnotic, Mind-bending Work of Italian Designer Franco Grignani” (2019)

lineage.note: Wikipedia’s Op art article says op art “perhaps more closely derives from the constructivist practices of the Bauhaus”, and that Moholy-Nagy taught optical exercises there. Josef Albers carried Bauhaus color and perception studies to Black Mountain College and Yale.
Wikipedia’s Op art article, citing MoMA, lists Constructivism with Neo-Impressionism, Cubism, Futurism, and Dada as antecedents of op art’s graphic effects.

lineage.label: Neo-Impressionism
lineage.note: Wikipedia names the Divisionists, who used optics to raise the luminosity of their paintings, as antecedents.

lineage.label: Kinetic art
lineage.note: Tate notes “the close connection between kinetic and op art”, for example in Soto’s work. Vasarely’s 1955 “Yellow manifesto” for the Mouvements exhibition joined optical and kinetic aims (Wikipedia).

Both peak in the mid-1960s and use contrast that makes edges vibrate. The [Psychedelic art](style:psychedelic-art) record gives the sources for the link through Albers and Moscoso. Psychedelic posters took the vibration and added figures, hand lettering, and saturated color.

grammar.text: Pure black on pure white, sometimes with a scale of grays. The maximum value contrast makes edges flicker. Color, when it appears, is one hue or a set of close tones, and it does not replace the black-and-white structure.
Parallel stripes, checkerboards, concentric circles, dots, and chevrons. Units are identical and repeat edge to edge. There are no figures or objects.

A regular pattern changes step by step: stripes narrow toward an edge, squares compress, or rings swell, so that the flat surface seems to bulge or sink. A field of one orientation meets a field of another, and the edge seems to float.
Flat, sharp, even paint or print with no texture, gradient, or shadow. Two fine patterns laid over each other at a small offset make moiré fringes.
The pattern runs to the edges of the canvas, the dress, or the page. In graphic design, a large pattern panel sits beside plain type, or type is cut out of the pattern.
Text is a neutral or condensed grotesque, set black on white. Display letters sometimes carry stripes or concentric outlines, as in Grignani’s work, but body text stays plain.
The motion is in the eye: after-images, shimmer, and swelling. On screen, a slow shift of pattern phase is the equivalent. Most op works are still.

diagnostic: Black-and-white stripes, checks, or rings fill a large area, edge to edge.
The pattern is tight and sharp enough that it seems to shimmer, swell, or move.
A regular unit changes by steps (narrows, compresses, bends) to suggest depth on a flat surface.
Two patterns overlap to make moiré, or two fields of different orientation meet at a hard edge.
Type, when present, is a plain sans-serif in black or white.
counter: Figures, faces, flowers, or other representational imagery carry the composition.
Soft gradients, drop shadows, gloss, or texture.
Several saturated hues side by side in large areas.
Isolated geometric shapes on a plain ground, with no repeating pattern.

confusions.difference: Psychedelic posters also vibrate, but with saturated complementary colors, melting hand lettering, and figures. Op art is abstract, mostly black and white, and built from ruled geometry.
The Swiss style also uses black, white, and sans-serif type, but relies on the grid and white space. Op art fills the surface with a repeating pattern that makes the eye see motion.

Memphis also uses black-and-white stripes and grids, but as one laminate among many clashing colors and irregular shapes. Op art keeps to black and white and to one precise, regular pattern at a time.
Bauhaus composes a few elementary shapes in primary colors. Op art repeats one unit many times until it becomes a field.
Kinetic works move physically, by motor, wind, or the viewer’s walk. Op art is still and makes the eye supply the motion.

do: Use pure black and pure white. Add grays only as steps in a scale.
Fill large panels edge to edge with one repeating pattern: stripes, checks, or rings.
Make the pattern change by steps, for example stripes that narrow or rings that swell, to suggest a bulge.
Put a field of one orientation inside a field of another, such as a horizontal-stripe disc on vertical stripes.
Overlap two fine patterns at a small offset for moiré in one place.
Put text on solid white or black panels with hard edges, never directly on the pattern.
Use a plain or condensed grotesque. Stripes inside large display letters are allowed.
Give patterns a fixed size so that the effect is the same at every width, and offer a calm alternative for people who are sensitive to it.
dont: Do not set body text, form fields, or table cells on top of stripes or checks.
Do not use gradients, drop shadows, glass, or gloss.
Do not add illustrations, photographs of people, or ornament to the pattern.
Do not use several saturated hues. One accent at most.
Do not animate patterns quickly or flash them. Fast flicker can trigger seizures.
avoid: Long reading and text-heavy interfaces. The patterns seem to move and strain the eyes.
Readers with vestibular or photosensitive conditions. Keep high-contrast stripes out of scrolling backgrounds and motion.

fingerprint.note: Positive marker. Repeating stripes, checks, or rings fill a large part of the page; the specimen measures 0.54. Pop art, Streamline Moderne, Vienna Secession, Skeuomorphism, and Grunge typography specimens also pass this range and fail on contrast, hue, lightness, or shadow. Provisional: set from the specimen; real sites often draw patterns as SVG or images, which this metric does not count. All three kept captures measure 0 because the pattern is an image; judge such sites by the rubric.
Positive marker. Many boxes, not only one backdrop, carry a pattern: cards, bands, and panels. The specimen measures 0.18. Provisional: set from the specimen.

synthesis: The black and white core runs from painting into mass products within about three years. Riley’s [Fall](ref:riley-fall-1963) and her [study for Intake](ref:riley-study-for-intake-1964) and Vasarely’s [Oeta](ref:vasarely-oeta-screenprint-1959) define the devices: one unit repeated edge to edge, changed by steps in width, period, or shape. By 1965–66 the same devices are on a [Biba mini-dress](ref:biba-op-art-mini-dress-1965), a [Scott paper dress](ref:scott-paper-op-art-paper-dress-1966), [Heal’s furnishing fabric](ref:barbara-brown-expansion-fabric-1966), and [screen-printed acrylic earrings](ref:ramshaw-watkins-optik-art-earrings).

Graphic design keeps text apart from the field. The [Responsive Eye catalogue](ref:the-responsive-eye-catalogue-1965) lets display letters carry Riley’s stripes but sets its title page plain; [McLaren’s CND poster](ref:mclaren-cnd-easter-67-poster) puts grotesque type on a solid black band above a swelling dot field. Grignani’s [Woolmark](ref:grignani-woolmark-logo-1964) shows that a few heavy tapering stripes survive at logo size. [Noll’s sinusoids](ref:noll-ninety-parallel-sinusoids-1964) show that the Riley wave is a rule that code can generate.

Few live websites use the style. The [Michèle Vasarely Foundation](ref:vasarely-com-website) is the clearest: a full-screen distorted grid with text only in black pills. [Marina Apollonio’s site](ref:marina-apollonio-website) uses a ring field as its hero; the [Grignani blog](ref:franco-grignani-info-website) is borderline. On all three the pattern is an image, so `color.patternShare` and `surface.patternShare` read 0, and the CSS lightness sees only the plain ground. The fingerprint now reads lightness from the screenshot. Judge image-drawn patterns by the rubric.

tokens.$description: Authored tokens for op-art. Shorthand values; tools/build.mjs writes DTCG 2025.10.

subtle.$description: Light gray: a second step in the scale.

primary.$description: Black: the figure. Op art works at the maximum value contrast.

secondary.$description: White: the ground, used as an inverted button and panel.

accent.$description: Mid gray: a step in Riley's gray scales, not a hue.

mono.$description: Labels use the body grotesque. The style has no monospaced voice.

pill.$description: Only for circles: discs and ring targets.

references.title: Alfieri & Lacroix advertising page
references.note: Grignani’s optical graphics before the term op art existed: distorted stripes fill a black page. Partial fit: a photographed figure and two colours are counter-traits.

references.title: Biba op-art mini-dress
references.note: An op print of nested diamonds on a mass-market dress. Partial fit: the colours are brown and black, not black and white.

references.title: Easter ’67 poster
references.note: Clear graphic-design use of op art: a black and white dot field that swells by steps, with plain sans-serif type in a separate band.

references.title: Expansion furnishing fabric
references.note: A clear op furnishing print: black and white stripes that change width by steps to suggest swelling and depth.

references.title: Fall
references.note: A canonical black and white op painting: one curved stripe repeated edge to edge, with a period that changes by steps to make the surface seem to move.

references.title: Franco Grignani blog
references.note: Borderline: black and white radial lines and a diagonal stripe band carry the page, but a photographed face, a gold script signature, and card shadows are counter-traits.

references.title: Marina Apollonio website
references.note: Clear in imagery: a wide black and white ring field that changes by steps, with plain sans-serif text kept off the pattern. A soft shadow under the next panel is a counter-trait.

references.title: Michèle Vasarely Foundation website
references.note: Clear: a black, white, and grey square grid fills the whole viewport and distorts by steps, and all text sits in solid black pills with plain sans-serif. The pattern is an image, so the pattern metrics read zero.

references.title: Ninety Parallel Sinusoids with Linearly Increasing Period
references.note: A computer plot built to reproduce the op effect of Riley’s wave paintings: parallel black lines on white whose period changes by steps.

references.title: Oeta – 1956
references.note: Vasarely’s black and white period in print: a regular grid of squares that bends into rhombs to suggest folding and depth.

references.title: Op-art paper dress
references.note: The black and white op check moved straight onto a cheap mass-market garment: an all-over field of squares that compress and expand.

references.title: Optik Art earrings
references.note: Black and white op geometry at the smallest scale: rings and squares nested so that figure and ground swap. Partial fit: a single motif, not an all-over field.

references.title: Study for the painting “Intake”
references.note: A clear black and white Riley study: stripes that change width and direction by steps, so the flat sheet seems to flow.

references.title: The Responsive Eye
references.note: The exhibition catalogue that fixed op art in public view, with a black and white Riley wave field as its cover.

references.title: Woolmark logo
references.note: Op-art line work compressed into a trademark: parallel black stripes that taper and curve so that a flat mark seems to turn. Partial fit: a single emblem, not an all-over field.
